claim: Migraine headache is hypothesized to involve the activation and sensitization of trigeminal sensory afferents that innervate the cranial meninges.
source: Migraine headache is hypothesized to involve the activation and sensitization of trigeminal sensory afferents that innervate the cranial meninges.
evidence: This is a statement about the current hypothesis in the field, supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: A single CSD episode caused a seconds-long wave of calcium activation that propagated across afferents and along the length of individual afferents.
source: A single CSD episode caused a seconds-long wave of calcium activation that propagated across afferents and along the length of individual afferents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript and shown in figures.

claim: Only a very small afferent population was persistently activated in the awake mouse preparation following CSD.
source: Surprisingly, unlike previous studies in anesthetized animals with exposed meninges, only a very small afferent population was persistently activated in our awake mouse preparation, questioning the relevance of this neuronal response to the onset of migraine pain.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data comparing findings in awake mice to previous studies in anesthetized animals.

claim: A larger subset of meningeal afferents developed augmented responses to acute three-dimensional meningeal deformations that occur in response to locomotion bouts following CSD.
source: In contrast, we identified a larger subset of meningeal afferents that developed augmented responses to acute three-dimensional meningeal deformations that occur in response to locomotion bouts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging and locomotion tracking.

claim: Increased responsiveness was observed in a subset of afferents that were already somewhat sensitive to meningeal deformation before CSD.
source: We observed increased responsiveness in a subset of afferents that were already somewhat sensitive to meningeal deformation before CSD.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of afferent responses before and after CSD.

claim: Another subset of previously insensitive afferents became sensitive to meningeal deformation following CSD.
source: Furthermore, another subset of previously insensitive afferents also became sensitive to meningeal deformation following CSD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing emergence of new responses.

claim: Enhanced meningeal afferent responses to movement-related meningeal deformations may be a potential neural substrate underlying the worsening of migraine headache during physical activity.
source: Our data provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying migraine, including the emergence of enhanced meningeal afferent responses to movement-related meningeal deformations as a potential neural substrate underlying the worsening of migraine headache during physical activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of migraine pathophysiology.

claim: Persistent discharge of meningeal afferents is thought to mediate the ongoing headache in migraine.
source: Persistent discharge of meningeal afferents is thought to mediate the ongoing headache, while their augmented mechanosensitivity has been suggested to underlie migraine headache exacerbation during normally innocuous physical activities that cause transient intracranial hypertension, such as coughing and other types of straining (Blau and Dexter, 1981).
evidence: This claim is based on established understanding in the field.

claim: Augmented mechanosensitivity of meningeal afferents has been suggested to underlie migraine headache exacerbation during normally innocuous physical activities that cause transient intracranial hypertension, such as coughing and other types of straining.
source: Persistent discharge of meningeal afferents is thought to mediate the ongoing headache, while their augmented mechanosensitivity has been suggested to underlie migraine headache exacerbation during normally innocuous physical activities that cause transient intracranial hypertension, such as coughing and other types of straining (Blau and Dexter, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cortical spreading depolarization (CSD) is a self-propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarizations thought to mediate migraine aura.
source: For example, triggering an episode of cortical spreading depolarization (CSD), a self-propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarizations thought to mediate migraine aura, causes persistent activation and mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents (Zhang et al., 2010; Zhao and Levy, 2015; Zhao and Levy, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of CSD based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Triggering an episode of CSD causes persistent activation and mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents.
source: For example, triggering an episode of cortical spreading depolarization (CSD), a self-propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarizations thought to mediate migraine aura, causes persistent activation and mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents (Zhang et al., 2010; Zhao and Levy, 2015; Zhao and Levy, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Prior studies on meningeal afferents have almost all used acute invasive experiments involving electrophysiological recordings in anesthetized animals with surgically exposed and mildly inflamed meninges.
source: Despite the preclinical evidence implicating enhanced responsiveness of meningeal afferents as a driver of migraine headache (Levy and Moskowitz, 2023), these studies have almost all used acute invasive experiments involving electrophysiological recordings in anesthetized animals with surgically exposed and mildly inflamed meninges (Levy et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on a review of previous literature.

claim: Studies documenting the mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents were based on findings of increased responsiveness to artificial compressive forces applied to the meninges of a depressurized brain.
source: Moreover, studies documenting the mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents were based on findings of increased responsiveness to artificial compressive forces applied to the meninges of a depressurized brain.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology of previous studies.

claim: There is a significant gap in our understanding of whether and how meningeal afferents respond to migraine-related events under more naturalistic conditions in behaving animals with an intact and pressurized intracranial space.
source: Hence, there is a significant gap in our understanding of whether and how meningeal afferents respond to migraine-related events under more naturalistic conditions in behaving animals with an intact and pressurized intracranial space.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of previous studies.

claim: The study used two-photon calcium imaging of meningeal afferent responses within the closed intracranial space of an awake-behaving mouse.
source: To better understand migraine pathophysiology and improve clinical translation, we leveraged a newly developed approach for two-photon calcium imaging of meningeal afferent responses within the closed intracranial space of an awake-behaving mouse (Blaeser et al., 2022d) in the CSD model of migraine.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: The study examined changes in afferent ongoing activity and afferent responses to three-dimensional (3D) meningeal deformation associated with locomotion following the triggering of a single CSD episode.
source: We studied changes in afferent ongoing activity and afferent responses to three-dimensional (3D) meningeal deformation associated with locomotion Blaeser et al., 2022d following the triggering of a single CSD episode.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Acute calcium signaling in meningeal afferent fibers may be a potentially critical nociceptive factor contributing to migraine pain.
source: Our data provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying migraine pathophysiology, including acute calcium signaling in meningeal afferent fibers as a potentially critical nociceptive factor contributing to migraine pain and the emergence of enhanced meningeal afferent responses to movement-related meningeal deformations as the neural substrate underlying the worsening of migraine headache during physical activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging was performed of GCaMP6s-expressing trigeminal afferent fibers innervating the meninges above the visual cortex (n=325 fibers from 9 fields of view [FOVs] from 7 mice).
source: To investigate meningeal afferent responses to CSD, we performed two-photon calcium imaging of GCaMP6s-expressing trigeminal afferent fibers innervating the meninges above the visual cortex (n=325 fibers from 9 fields of view [FOVs] from 7 mice, Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and sample size.

claim: A single CSD episode was triggered in the frontal cortex with a cortical pinprick.
source: We triggered a single CSD episode in the frontal cortex with a cortical pinprick.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: In every experiment (9 CSDs in 7 mice), a slow, CSD-like wave of calcium activity was detected in numerous meningeal afferent fibers within 1 min following the pinprick.
source: In every experiment (9 CSDs in 7 mice), we detected a slow, CSD-like wave of calcium activity in numerous meningeal afferent fibers within 1 min following the pinprick (Figure 1B, Figure 1—video 1) as well as in background regions (likely reflecting signal from small, out-of-focus afferent branches).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Calcium waves were also detected in background regions, likely reflecting signal from small, out-of-focus afferent branches.
source: In every experiment (9 CSDs in 7 mice), we detected a slow, CSD-like wave of calcium activity in numerous meningeal afferent fibers within 1 min following the pinprick (Figure 1B, Figure 1—video 1) as well as in background regions (likely reflecting signal from small, out-of-focus afferent branches).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed signal.

claim: Calcium waves proceeded from the pinprick site in an anterior-to-posterior direction across the FOV.
source: These calcium waves proceeded from the pinprick site in an anterior-to-posterior direction across the FOV (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Progressive activation of portions of individual afferent fibers aligned to the wave's movement direction was observed.
source: We also observed progressive activation of portions of individual afferent fibers aligned to the wave's movement direction.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: The sequential recruitment of ROIs along an afferent fiber during the CSD-like wave was much slower compared to baseline afferent calcium signals observed during periods of locomotion.
source: Compared to baseline afferent calcium signals observed during periods of locomotion, during which all ROIs belonging to an afferent were activated near-simultaneously, as previously reported (Blaeser et al., 2022d), the sequential recruitment of ROIs along an afferent fiber during the CSD-like wave was much slower (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental observations.

claim: During locomotion bouts, all ROIs belonging to an afferent were activated near-simultaneously.
source: Compared to baseline afferent calcium signals observed during periods of locomotion, during which all ROIs belonging to an afferent were activated near-simultaneously, as previously reported (Blaeser et al., 2022d), the sequential recruitment of ROIs along an afferent fiber during the CSD-like wave was much slower (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This is a reference to a previous finding.

claim: The proportion of afferents activated during the CSD-like wave exceeded the proportion activated during locomotion bouts.
source: The proportion of afferents activated during this period exceeded the proportion activated during locomotion bouts (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of activation during the CSD-like wave was larger than during locomotion.
source: The magnitude of activation was also larger (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the experimental data.

claim: On average, the CSD-associated calcium wave progressed at 3.8±0.2 mm/min.
source: On average, the wave progressed at 3.8±0.2 mm/min.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: CSD gives rise to acute neuronal and glial swelling and shrinkage of the cortical extracellular space.
source: CSD gives rise to acute neuronal and glial swelling and shrinkage of the cortical extracellular space (Mazel et al., 2002; Takano et al., 2007; Rosic et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement based on previous literature.

claim: Cortical mechanical perturbations from CSD could lead to acute meningeal deformation.
source: Such cortical mechanical perturbations could lead to acute meningeal deformation, which we have shown previously can activate mechanosensitive meningeal afferents (Blaeser et al., 2022d).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings.

claim: Meningeal deformation can activate mechanosensitive meningeal afferents.
source: Such cortical mechanical perturbations could lead to acute meningeal deformation, which we have shown previously can activate mechanosensitive meningeal afferents (Blaeser et al., 2022d).
evidence: This is a reference to a previous finding.

claim: Severe meningeal scaling and shearing were observed during the CSD-evoked afferent calcium wave (6 CSDs in 6 mice).
source: Assessment of meningeal deformation parameters (see Materials and methods) revealed severe meningeal scaling and shearing during the CSD-evoked afferent calcium wave (6 CSDs in 6 mice, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: The temporal pattern of meningeal shearing somewhat resembled that of the acute afferent response in some experiments.
source: In some experiments, the temporal pattern of meningeal shearing (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) somewhat resembled that of the acute afferent response.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The pattern of meningeal scaling was incongruent with the acute afferent response.
source: However, the pattern of meningeal scaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) was incongruent with the acute afferent response.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The direction of Z-shifts in the meninges during the CSD-evoked calcium wave was inconsistent across mice.
source: Surprisingly, the direction of Z-shifts in the meninges during this epoch was inconsistent across mice, resulting in no significant Z-shift on average relative to the pre-CSD epoch (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant Z-shift on average relative to the pre-CSD epoch.
source: Surprisingly, the direction of Z-shifts in the meninges during this epoch was inconsistent across mice, resulting in no significant Z-shift on average relative to the pre-CSD epoch (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: A general linear model (GLM) was used to estimate the relative contribution of CSD-driven meningeal deformation to the acute afferent responses.
source: To estimate the relative contribution of the CSD-driven meningeal deformation to the acute afferent responses we observed, we used a general linear model (GLM; see Blaeser et al., 2022d, and Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used.

claim: The analysis focused on afferents whose pre-CSD (baseline) activity could be predicted by the GLM based on deformation predictors (n=145 afferents from 6 mice).
source: We focused on afferents whose pre-CSD (baseline) activity could be predicted by the GLM based on deformation predictors (n=145 afferents from 6 mice).
evidence: This describes the subset of data analyzed.

claim: There was a poor match between the real peri-CSD calcium signals and those predicted by the GLMs trained using pre-CSD deformation data.
source: Overall, we observed a poor match between the real peri-CSD calcium signals and those predicted by the GLMs trained using pre-CSD deformation data (see example in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and summary GLM fits in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), suggesting that the model poorly predicted the magnitude of the activity and/or its temporal pattern in response to CSD.
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: The GLM poorly predicted the magnitude of the activity and/or its temporal pattern in response to CSD.
source: Overall, we observed a poor match between the real peri-CSD calcium signals and those predicted by the GLMs trained using pre-CSD deformation data (see example in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and summary GLM fits in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), suggesting that the model poorly predicted the magnitude of the activity and/or its temporal pattern in response to CSD.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GLM results.

claim: Approximately 95% of the afferents were acutely activated by CSD.
source: Because ~95% of the afferents were acutely activated by CSD (Figure 1I), we propose that this response is mostly driven by other non-mechanical factors, such as the local depolarizing effects of diffusible excitatory molecules.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The acute afferent response to CSD is mostly driven by other non-mechanical factors, such as the local depolarizing effects of diffusible excitatory molecules.
source: Because ~95% of the afferents were acutely activated by CSD (Figure 1I), we propose that this response is mostly driven by other non-mechanical factors, such as the local depolarizing effects of diffusible excitatory molecules.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: In anesthetized rats with exposed meninges, CSD drives sustained increases in ongoing activity lasting tens of minutes in ~50% of meningeal afferents.
source: In anesthetized rats with exposed meninges, CSD drives sustained increases in ongoing activity lasting tens of minutes in ~50% of meningeal afferents (Zhao and Levy, 2015).
evidence: This is a reference to a previous finding.

claim: The study assessed CSD-related changes in afferent ongoing activity in awake mice with intact meninges by focusing on afferent responses during epochs of immobility between locomotion bouts (8 CSDs in 7 mice).
source: To directly assess CSD-related changes in afferent ongoing activity in awake mice with intact meninges, we focused on afferent responses during epochs of immobility between locomotion bouts (8 CSDs in 7 mice).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Low levels of ongoing activity were observed at baseline before CSD (fluorescent events occurring 6.9 ± 0.3% of the time).
source: We observed low levels of ongoing activity at baseline before CSD (fluorescent events occurring 6.9 ± 0.3% of the time), consistent with our previous study in naïve mice (Blaeser et al., 2022d).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Most afferents (~70%, 201/288) did not display any change in ongoing activity during the 2 hr following CSD.
source: Unexpectedly, most afferents (~70%, 201/288) did not display any change in ongoing activity during the 2 hr following CSD (termed 'post-CSD').
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Sustained increases in ongoing activity were identified in ~10% (30/288) of the afferents during the 2 hr following CSD.
source: However, we identified sustained increases in ongoing activity in ~10% (30/288) of the afferents during this period.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: A larger afferent population (~20%; 57/288) showed suppressed activity following CSD.
source: Surprisingly, we also observed a larger afferent population (~20%; 57/288) whose activity was suppressed (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Afferents with sustained activation showed increased ongoing activity that emerged at an ~25 min delay on average.
source: Afferents with sustained activation showed increased ongoing activity that emerged at an ~25 min delay on average (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Afferents with sustained suppression showed decreases in ongoing activity beginning shortly after the passage of the acute calcium wave.
source: In contrast, afferents with sustained suppression showed decreases in ongoing activity beginning shortly after the passage of the acute calcium wave (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: The durations of the afferent activation or suppression were similar, lasting ~25 min on average.
source: The durations of the afferent activation or suppression were similar, lasting ~25 min on average (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Meningeal deformation associated with locomotion bouts can lead to the activation of mechanosensitive meningeal afferents.
source: Meningeal deformation associated with locomotion bouts can lead to the activation of mechanosensitive meningeal afferents (Blaeser et al., 2022d).
evidence: This is a reference to a previous finding.

claim: CSD suppresses cortical activity, leading to decreased motor function.
source: CSD suppresses cortical activity, leading to decreased motor function (Houben et al., 2017), including reduced locomotion in head-fixed mice (Enger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement based on previous literature.

claim: CSD leads to reduced locomotion in head-fixed mice.
source: CSD suppresses cortical activity, leading to decreased motor function (Houben et al., 2017), including reduced locomotion in head-fixed mice (Enger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement based on previous literature.

claim: CSD-related vascular changes and reduced extracellular space could affect meningeal deformations and the associated afferent response.
source: CSD-related vascular changes and reduced extracellular space (Mazel et al., 2002; Takano et al., 2007) could also affect meningeal deformations and the associated afferent response.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings.

claim: In most sessions, mice stopped locomoting following the CSD (8/9 CSDs in 7 mice).
source: In most sessions, mice stopped locomoting following the CSD (8/9 CSDs in 7 mice) but resumed sporadic wheel running activity ~6 min later on average (range 0.5–16.5 min).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Mice resumed sporadic wheel running activity ~6 min after CSD on average (range 0.5–16.5 min).
source: In most sessions, mice stopped locomoting following the CSD (8/9 CSDs in 7 mice) but resumed sporadic wheel running activity ~6 min later on average (range 0.5–16.5 min).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Mice ran less during the 2 hr following CSD than during the baseline period.
source: However, the mice ran less during the 2 hr following CSD than during the baseline period (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from the experimental data.

claim: There was an overall reduction in bout rate during the post-CSD period.
source: Locomotion bout analysis also revealed an overall reduction in bout rate during the post-CSD period (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: CSD had minimal effect on locomotion bout characteristics, including bout duration and peak velocity.
source: Remarkably, despite the reduction in locomotion following CSD, we observed similar bout characteristics at baseline and post-CSD, including bout duration (Figure 3D) and peak velocity (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: CSD did not affect bout-related meningeal deformations: similar scaling, shearing, and Z-shift values were observed during the 2 hr post-CSD.
source: Surprisingly, CSD did not affect bout-related meningeal deformations: we observed similar scaling, shearing, and Z-shift values during the 2 hr post-CSD (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: Initial observations indicated enhanced afferent responsiveness during locomotion following CSD.
source: Initial observations of afferent activation during locomotion indicated enhanced responsiveness following CSD (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: GLMs were used to assess whether meningeal afferent activity becomes sensitized to the state of locomotion and/or to various aspects of meningeal deformation following CSD.
source: To systematically investigate this augmented afferent response, we used GLMs (see Materials and methods and Blaeser et al., 2022d) to assess whether meningeal afferent activity becomes sensitized to the state of locomotion and/or to various aspects of meningeal deformation following CSD.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used.

claim: Each afferent's activity was modeled based on variables that describe (1) the binary state of locomotion, (2) mouse velocity, or (3) aspects of meningeal deformation, including scaling, shearing, and Z-shift.
source: We modeled each afferent's activity based on variables that describe (1) the binary state of locomotion, (2) mouse velocity, or (3) aspects of meningeal deformation, including scaling, shearing, and Z-shift.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach.

claim: The analysis focused on afferents whose activity could be predicted by the same variables both at baseline and following CSD (n=67/325 afferents, 9 CSDs in 7 mice).
source: We first focused on afferents whose activity could be predicted by the same variables both at baseline and following CSD (i.e. afferents that exhibited sensitivities to locomotion and/or deformation signals both before and after CSD, n=67/325 afferents, 9 CSDs in 7 mice).
evidence: This describes the subset of data analyzed.

claim: An afferent was defined as sensitized by CSD if its GLM coefficients post-CSD were larger than at baseline.
source: Thus, we defined an afferent as sensitized by CSD if its GLM coefficients post-CSD were larger than at baseline (i.e. stronger activation of afferents per unit deformation or locomotion; for example, see Figure 4C).
evidence: This defines the criterion for sensitization.

claim: Elevated locomotion and/or deformation-related activity (i.e. sensitization) post-CSD was identified in ~51% of afferents (34/67).
source: Using these criteria, we identified elevated locomotion and/or deformation-related activity (i.e. sensitization) post-CSD in ~51% of afferents (34/67; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the GLM analysis.

claim: Only 12% of afferents (8/67) showed reduced locomotion- and deformation-related activity (i.e. desensitization) post-CSD.
source: In contrast, only 12% of afferents (8/67) showed reduced locomotion- and deformation-related activity (i.e. desensitization) post-CSD.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the GLM analysis.

claim: Sensitivity was unchanged in 37% of afferents (25/67).
source: Sensitivity was unchanged in the remaining 37% of afferents (25/67).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the GLM analysis.

claim: Only the deformation coefficients were increased post-CSD in sensitized afferents.
source: Surprisingly, we found that only the deformation coefficients were increased post-CSD (Figure 4E), suggesting that meningeal afferent sensitization following CSD reflects primarily an increased sensitivity to local mechanical deformations.
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: Meningeal afferent sensitization following CSD reflects primarily an increased sensitivity to local mechanical deformations.
source: Surprisingly, we found that only the deformation coefficients were increased post-CSD (Figure 4E), suggesting that meningeal afferent sensitization following CSD reflects primarily an increased sensitivity to local mechanical deformations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GLM results.

claim: Among the 245 afferents that were not well fit before CSD (i.e. insensitive), a substantial population (53/245) developed a sensitivity to locomotion and deformation variables following CSD.
source: Indeed, among the 245 afferents that were not well fit before CSD (i.e. insensitive), we detected a substantial population that developed a sensitivity to locomotion and deformation variables following CSD (53/245; i.e. afferents whose activity could be well predicted by locomotion and deformation variables following CSD).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the GLM analysis.

claim: Far fewer neurons (13/245) lost their sensitivity to locomotion and deformation variables after CSD.
source: By contrast, far fewer neurons (13/245) lost their sensitivity to these variables after CSD (i.e. afferents that were well fit before but not after CSD).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the GLM analysis.

claim: Four times more afferents displayed increased sensitivity than decreased sensitivity following CSD (87 vs 21 afferents).
source: Overall, the above findings show that four times more afferents displayed increased sensitivity than decreased sensitivity following CSD (87 vs 21 afferents).
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative results.

claim: The sensitized afferent population displayed post-CSD increases in GLM coefficients related to deformation but not to locomotion.
source: This sensitized afferent population also displayed post-CSD increases in GLM coefficients related to deformation but not to locomotion (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: The impact of deformation variables on the model fit was greater post-CSD than pre-CSD.
source: We found that the impact of deformation variables on the model fit was greater post-CSD than pre-CSD, while the impact of locomotion variables was similar pre- and post-CSD.
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: The impact of locomotion variables on the model fit was similar pre- and post-CSD.
source: We found that the impact of deformation variables on the model fit was greater post-CSD than pre-CSD, while the impact of locomotion variables was similar pre- and post-CSD.
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: The finding that deformation variables had greater impact post-CSD was true for afferents with models that were well fit both at baseline and following CSD.
source: This was true for afferents with models that were well fit both at baseline and following CSD (Figure 4G; purple subset in Figure 4D) and for those with models that were well fit only post-CSD (Figure 4H; magenta subset in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: The finding that deformation variables had greater impact post-CSD was true for afferents with models that were well fit only post-CSD.
source: This was true for afferents with models that were well fit both at baseline and following CSD (Figure 4G; purple subset in Figure 4D) and for those with models that were well fit only post-CSD (Figure 4H; magenta subset in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: Scale, shear, and Z-shift deformations were, on average, equally important in predicting the activity patterns of sensitized afferents.
source: Further analysis revealed that scale, shear, and Z-shift deformations were, on average, equally important in predicting the activity patterns of sensitized afferents (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: The afferent sensitization following CSD primarily involves increased afferent responsiveness to a mix of meningeal deformation variables rather than to other locomotion-associated processes.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the afferent sensitization following CSD primarily involves increased afferent responsiveness to a mix of meningeal deformation variables rather than to other locomotion-associated processes.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the GLM results.

claim: Previous studies in anesthetized rats suggested that the mechanisms underlying meningeal afferent mechanical sensitization are independent of those responsible for increased ongoing discharge in several migraine models, including CSD.
source: Previous studies in anesthetized rats suggested that the mechanisms underlying meningeal afferent mechanical sensitization are independent of those responsible for increased ongoing discharge in several migraine models, including CSD (Levy and Strassman, 2002; Zhang et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2013; Zhao and Levy, 2018; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a reference to previous findings.

claim: Using the CSD model in awake mice, no association was found between sensitization and sustained changes in ongoing activity.
source: Here, using the CSD model in awake mice, we also found no association between sensitization and sustained changes in ongoing activity, as similar proportions of sensitized and non-sensitized afferents were activated, suppressed, or did not display any change in their ongoing activity following CSD (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a result from the experimental data.

claim: Similar proportions of sensitized and non-sensitized afferents were activated, suppressed, or did not display any change in their ongoing activity following CSD.
source: Here, using the CSD model in awake mice, we also found no association between sensitization and sustained changes in ongoing activity, as similar proportions of sensitized and non-sensitized afferents were activated, suppressed, or did not display any change in their ongoing activity following CSD (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Prior studies suggested that CSD drives meningeal nociception that can lead to the headache phase in migraine with aura.
source: Prior studies suggested that CSD drives meningeal nociception that can lead to the headache phase in migraine with aura.
evidence: This is a reference to previous understanding in the field.

claim: Prior studies mostly involved invasive experiments in anesthetized rats with surgically exposed meninges, showing prolonged activation and mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents.
source: These studies, which mostly involved invasive experiments in anesthetized rats with surgically exposed meninges, showed prolonged activation and mechanical sensitization of meningeal afferents (Carneiro-Nascimento and Levy, 2022).
evidence: This is a reference to previous studies.

claim: The current study used two-photon calcium imaging to characterize, for the first time, CSD-related changes in the responsiveness of individual meningeal sensory afferents at the level of their peripheral nerve fibers in the closed cranium of a behaving mouse.
source: To better understand migraine pathophysiology and improve clinical translation, we used two-photon calcium imaging to characterize, for the first time, CSD-related changes in the responsiveness of individual meningeal sensory afferents at the level of their peripheral nerve fibers in the closed cranium of a behaving mouse.
evidence: This describes the novelty of the current study.

claim: A single CSD episode drives a wave of calcium activity across most afferents while producing a more prolonged change in ongoing activity in only a small subset.
source: We show that a single CSD episode drives a wave of calcium activity across most afferents while producing a more prolonged change in ongoing activity in only a small subset.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The study combined afferent calcium imaging with behavioral tracking of locomotion and estimates of local meningeal deformations.
source: We then combined afferent calcium imaging with behavioral tracking of locomotion and estimates of local meningeal deformations.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: CSD causes prolonged augmentation of afferent responsiveness to meningeal deformations associated with locomotion in previously sensitive afferents.
